Corn
KōRN
n. (rendering Hebrew dāgān and bār, Greek sitos and kokkos)
From Old English corn, cognate with Latin granum, a grain. In the King James Version and in British usage generally, corn means grain of any kind — wheat, barley, spelt — and never the American maize, which was unknown in the ancient Near East and in 1611. This is one of the archaisms most likely to mislead a modern reader: the fields the disciples walked through were fields of wheat.

Biblical Definition

Corn is grain, the staple of life, and Scripture uses it for the ordinary providence by which God feeds the world and for the extraordinary way He saves it. In the famine it is the commodity that draws the nations to the man they had sold into slavery: “And all countries came into Egypt to Joseph for to buy corn; because that the famine was so sore in all lands” (Gen 41:57) — the brothers' treachery becoming the means of the world's bread. The law surrounding corn is notable for its gentleness toward the labourer, including the animal one: “Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn” (Deu 25:4), a verse Paul twice applies to the maintenance of gospel ministers, arguing that God's care in such a matter was written for our sakes. The growth of corn is the Lord's figure for the hidden, unforced progress of the kingdom: “For the earth bringeth forth fruit of herself; first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear” (Mar 4:28) — a sequence no farmer can hurry and none can fully explain. And the cornfield is the setting of one of the great sabbath controversies, where hunger, mercy, and the Lord's authority over the day are all at issue at once: “At that time Jesus went on the sabbath day through the corn; and his disciples were an hungred, and began to pluck the ears of corn, and to eat” (Mat 12:1). The single grain finally becomes the figure of His own death, for except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone.

Webster 1828 Definition

Grain of any kind — wheat, barley, rye — and never maize in the Authorized Version; in Scripture the staple of life, the sheaf of the firstfruits, the field of the sabbath controversy, and the single grain that must die to bear fruit.

expand to see more

CORN, n. 1. A single seed of certain plants, as wheat, rye, barley and maize; a grain.

2. In Great Britain, corn is a general term for all sorts of grain used for bread; wheat, rye, barley and oats.

3. The plants which produce corn, when growing in the field; as a field of corn.

4. In Scripture usage, grain in general; the harvest of the field, the staple of bread. Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn. Deut. 25.

5. Corn and wine and oil; the standing summary of the produce of the land, and a token of covenant blessing. Deut. 7.

Key Scripture

Genesis 41:57 — "And all countries came into Egypt to Joseph for to buy corn; because that the famine was so sore in all lands."

Deuteronomy 25:4 — "Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn."

Mark 4:28 — "For the earth bringeth forth fruit of herself; first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear."

Matthew 12:1 — "At that time Jesus went on the sabbath day through the corn; and his disciples were an hungred, and began to pluck the ears of corn, and to eat."

Modern Corruption

The ordinary providence by which God feeds the world through seedtime and harvest is treated as an impersonal mechanism, so that daily bread ceases to be received as a gift and thanksgiving becomes a formality.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live corruption is practical secularism about food. Because the process from seed to loaf is understood, it is felt to be self-explaining, and the hand of God is looked for only in what science has not yet accounted for — a habit which shrinks God into the gaps and guarantees His steady eviction. Scripture never distinguishes the ordinary from the divine in this way. The Lord Jesus, teaching men to ask for daily bread, was speaking to farmers who knew exactly how wheat grows, and He grounds the doctrine of providence in the most regular phenomena there are: God maketh his sun to rise, sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust, and clothes the grass of the field. Mar 4:28 explicitly presents the growth of corn as something that happens while the farmer sleeps and which he knoweth not how — the mechanism understood and the giving still God's.

The principle to recover is that thanksgiving is the appropriate response to a mechanism, not a substitute for understanding one. Paul makes the refusal of thanks a mark of the fallen mind — when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful — and commends every creature of God as good if it be received with thanksgiving. There is a second recovery in Deu 25:4: God legislates for the comfort of an ox on a threshing floor, and Paul argues from that verse to the support of ministers, which tells us both that no detail of God's law is beneath notice and that the God who will not have an ox muzzled at his work does not intend His servants to labour unfed.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew dāgān is corn or grain generally, standing with wine and oil for the produce of the land; bār is threshed grain. Greek sitos is wheat or grain, and kokkos is a single seed or kernel.

expand to see more

Hebrew dāgān (H1715) — corn, grain; paired with tīrōsh (new wine) and yits'hār (oil) as the produce of the land.

Hebrew bār (H1250) — threshed and winnowed grain; the corn Joseph stored and sold (Gen 41:57).

Hebrew 'ābīb (H24) — green ears of corn; whence the month Abib, the month of ripening ears, in which the Passover falls.

Greek sitos (G4621) — wheat or grain; gather the wheat into my barn (Mat 13:30).

Greek kokkos (G2848) — a grain or kernel; except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die (Joh 12:24).

Usage

"Of providence in famine: all countries came into Egypt to Joseph for to buy corn (Gen 41:57)."

"Of mercy to the labouring beast: thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn (Deu 25:4)."

"Of the kingdom's hidden growth: first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear (Mar 4:28)."
